## Background.
The data being analyzed includes the Utah Pollinator Pursuit Dataset and an iNaturalist Dataset. The data only include records being collected in Utah from 2020 to 2023. The data was inspected for errors, which included unifying the species concepts. Bombus californicus was treated as B. fervidus; B. bifarius and B. vancouverensis were treated as B. bifarius/B. vancouverensis.

```{r warning=FALSE, include=FALSE}

# Load data and adjust Pollinator Pursuit data set
# setwd("/Users/jonathankoch/Library/CloudStorage/Box-Box/0_Collaborative Projects/Amanda Barth/Barth_TeamUtahBombus/0_WorkingAnalysis/Data_v2")
# list.files()

# Replace 'path_to_your_file.xlsx' with the actual path to your Excel file
df <- read_excel("UPP Bombus 2020-2023 cleaned_withoutsonorusinSLC.xlsx", sheet = "Sheet1")
names(df)

# Separate the 'date' column into 'year', 'month', and 'day' columns
df <- df %>%
  separate(`Observation Date`, into = c("year", "month", "day"), sep = "-")

# Create a date object
df$date <- as.Date(with(df, paste(year, month, day, sep = "-")), "%Y-%m-%d")

# Calculate Julian day numbers
df$julian_day <- as.numeric(strftime(df$date, format = "%j"))
names(df)

df <- df %>%
  mutate(`Bombus species` = ifelse(`Bombus species` == "bifarius", "vancouverensis/bifarius", `Bombus species`))

# Add a column that identifies this data as Utah Pollinator Pursuit data (UtahPP)
df$source <- "UtahPP"

nrow(df)
```

```{r warning=FALSE, include=FALSE}
# Load the iNaturalist datset
df_inat <- read_excel("iNat Bombus 2020-2023 cleaned.xlsx", sheet = "Sheet1")

names(df_inat)

# Separate the 'date' column into 'year', 'month', and 'day' columns
df_inat <- df_inat %>%
  separate(`Observation Date`, into = c("year", "month", "day"), sep = "-")
# Create a date object
df_inat$date <- as.Date(with(df_inat, paste(year, month, day, sep = "-")), "%Y-%m-%d")

# Calculate Julian day numbers
df_inat$julian_day <- as.numeric(strftime(df_inat$date, format = "%j"))
names(df_inat)

df_inat$source <- "iNat"

df_inat <- df_inat %>%
  mutate(`Bombus species` = ifelse(`Bombus species` == "californicus", "fervidus", `Bombus species`))

df_inat <- df_inat %>%
  mutate(`Bombus species` = ifelse(`Bombus species` == "vancouverensis nearcticus", "vancouverensis/bifarius", `Bombus species`))

df_inat <- df_inat %>%
  mutate(`Bombus species` = ifelse(`Bombus species` == "bifarius", "vancouverensis/bifarius", `Bombus species`))

df_inat <- df_inat %>%
  mutate(`Bombus species` = ifelse(`Bombus species` == "vancouverensis", "vancouverensis/bifarius", `Bombus species`))

df_inat <- df_inat %>% filter(`Bombus species` != "Bombus")
nrow(df_inat)
```

```{r}
# Combine datasets
names(df)
names(df_inat)

df_upp <- df %>% dplyr::select("year", "month", "day", "Bombus species",
                        "x", "y", "julian_day", "source")
df_upp <- df_upp %>% dplyr::filter(year %in% c(2020, 2021, 2022, 2023))


df_inat <- df_inat %>% dplyr::select("year", "month", "day", "Bombus species",
                        "x", "y", "julian_day", "source")
df_inat <- df_inat %>% dplyr::filter(year %in% c(2020, 2021, 2022, 2023))

df_all <- rbind(df_upp,df_inat)
nrow(df_all)
```

```{r include=FALSE}
# Add elevation to all the data
coordinates_df <- dplyr::select(df_all,"x", "y")
coordinates_df <-as.data.frame(coordinates_df)
names(coordinates_df)
nrow(coordinates_df)

# Combine latitude and longitude columns into a POINT geometry
coordinates_sf <- st_as_sf(coordinates_df, coords = c("x", "y"))

# Assign a CRS (e.g., WGS84, which is commonly used for GPS coordinates)
st_crs(coordinates_sf) <- st_crs("+proj=longlat +datum=WGS84")


elevation_data <- get_elev_point(coordinates_df, prj = "+proj=longlat +datum=WGS84", src = "aws")

df_all <-cbind(df_all,elevation_data)
nrow(df_all)
```

```{r include=FALSE}
# Load Ecoregion shapefile

# Replace "your_shapefile.shp" with the path to your shapefile
shapefile <- st_read("ut_eco_l3")
st_crs(coordinates_sf)
st_crs(shapefile)
shapefile_transformed <- st_transform(shapefile, crs = st_crs(coordinates_sf))

# Make sure the two files have same CRS
st_crs(shapefile_transformed)
st_crs(coordinates_sf)

result <- st_join(coordinates_sf, shapefile_transformed, left = TRUE)

# Read the KML file (assuming it contains polygon data) - this is the Utah Grid
# load kml data
kml_file <- "Utah Grid Cells.kml"

# Read the KML file using sf
kml_data <- st_read(kml_file)

# Ensure both layers have the same CRS
polygons_sf <- st_transform(kml_data, crs = st_crs(coordinates_sf))

# Perform a spatial join to assign polygon attributes to points where they intersect
joined_sf <- st_join(coordinates_sf, polygons_sf, join = st_intersects)

nrow(result)
df_all <-cbind(df_all,result)
df_all <-cbind(df_all, joined_sf)
df_all <-as.data.frame(df_all)
df_all <- subset(df_all, select = -geometry)
# df_all <- subset(df_all, select = -geometry)
write.csv(df_all, "df_all.csv", row.names = FALSE)
```

## Question 5b: Visualize the number of individuals of each species detected in the Utah Pollinator Pursuit and iNaturalist datasets,

```{r warning=FALSE,echo=FALSE, message=FALSE}

# Create a table of count data across species and data set type.
df_final_count <- df_final %>%
  group_by(`Bombus species`,source) %>%
  summarise(count = n()) %>%
  arrange(desc(count))

# Create a bar plot using ggplot2
ggplot(df_final_count, aes(x = reorder(`Bombus species`, -count), y = count, fill = source)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity", position = "dodge") +
  labs(title = "Count of individuals detected across species and data sets in Utah (2020-2023)",
       x = "Species",
       y = "Count of individuals",
       fill = "Data set") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 90, hjust = 1))

Fig1A <- ggplot(df_final_count, aes(x = reorder(`Bombus species`, -count), y = count, fill = source)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity", position = "dodge", color = "black") + # Black border
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("white", "grey")) +
  labs(x = "Species",
       y = "Count of individuals",
       fill = "Data set") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 90, hjust = 1, size=14))

ggsave("Figures/Fig1a.png", plot = Fig1A, width = 10, height = 8, units = "in")

```

In this graph iNaturalist data are the pink bars and the Utah Pollinator Pursuit data are the blue bars. The data is organized from most abundant species to least abundant species. The most abundant species in the iNaturalist data set are B. huntii, B. griseocollis, and B. fervidus. The most abundant species in the Utah Pollinator Pursuit data set are B. huntii, B. griseocollis, and B. vancouverensis/B. bifarius.

Is there a significant difference in the number of observations per species across years for UtahPP?
```{r warning=FALSE, echo=FALSE}

df_final_count_upp <- df_final %>%
  filter(source=="UtahPP")
nrow(df_final_count_upp)

# Create a contingency table of the data.
contingency_table <- table(df_final_count_upp$`Bombus species`, df_final_count_upp$year)
contingency_table

# Remove specific rows by index (e.g., remove 3rd and 4th rows)
contingency_table_filtered <- contingency_table[-c(8,9,12,13,15,16), ]

# Display the filtered table
print(contingency_table_filtered)
```

Why is there a difference; there might be a year effect; perhaps strongly observed in B. bifarius, B. appositus, B. insularis (2023)?

We answered this question with a Chi-square test.

```{r warning=FALSE, echo=FALSE}

# Perform chi-square test.
chi_square_result <- chisq.test(contingency_table_filtered)

# Print the results of the chi-square test.
print(chi_square_result)

library(vcd)
cramer_v <- assocstats(contingency_table)$cramer
print(cramer_v)

```
```{r warning=FALSE, echo=FALSE}
# Calculate Pearson residuals
residuals <- chi_square_result$residuals

# Print residuals
print(residuals)

# Identify cells with large residuals
significant_cells <- which(abs(residuals) > 2, arr.ind = TRUE)

# Convert residuals to a dataframe for plotting
res_df <- as.data.frame(as.table(residuals))

# Create a heatmap of residuals
ggplot(res_df, aes(Var1, Var2, fill = Freq)) +
  geom_tile(color = "white") +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = "blue", high = "red", mid = "white", midpoint = 0, limit = c(-12, 12)) +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.2f", Freq)), color = "black", angle=90) +
  labs(x = "Species", y = "Year", title = "Residuals of Chi-Square Test") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 90, hjust = 1))

ggplot(res_df, aes(Var1, Var2, fill = Freq)) +
  geom_tile(color = "white") +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = "white", high = "darkgrey", mid = "lightgrey", midpoint = 0, limit = c(-12, 12)) +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.2f", Freq)), color = "black", angle=90) +
  labs(x = "Species", y = "Year", title = "UtahPP Residuals of Chi-Square Test") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 90, hjust = 1, size=14),
        axis.text.y = element_text(size=14))
```

## Is there a difference between the number of species detected between the two data sets?

To answer this question, I generated a contingency table of the data collected. I then used a Chi-square test to determine if there is a significant association between the number of each species detected in Utah and the two community science approaches (Utah Pollinator Pursuit vs. iNaturalist). I then examined the standardized Chi-square test residuals to determine which data set and species are the biggest contributors to rejecting the null hypothesis. The null hypothesis is that there is no significant association between the number of individuals detected per species and the citizen science approach. The alternative hypothesis is that there is a significant association between the number of individuals detected per species and the citizen science approach.

```{r warning=FALSE, echo=FALSE}

# Create a contingency table of the data.
contingency_table <- table(df_final$`Bombus species`, df_final$source)
contingency_table
```

The contingency table shows some species were detected less than 5 times, which may cause the Chi-square approximation to be incorrect, and violate the assumptions of the Chi-square test. Thus, we elected to remove species that had <5 observations in a data set. We elected to remove 4 species: B. kirbiellus, B. melanopygus, B. mixtus, B. sonorus, and B. sylvicola.

Filtered contingency table to remove low frequency species.
```{r warning=FALSE, echo=FALSE}
# Remove specific rows by index (e.g., remove 3rd and 4th rows)
contingency_table_filtered <- contingency_table[-c(8,9,10,16,17), ]

# Display the filtered table
print(contingency_table_filtered)
```

##Is there a sigificant difference in the association between the two categorical variables (Species & Data set)? 

We answered this question with a Chi-square test.

```{r warning=FALSE, echo=FALSE}

# Perform chi-square test.
chi_square_result <- chisq.test(contingency_table_filtered)

# Print the results of the chi-square test.
print(chi_square_result)
```
No warnings were generated from the Chi-square test. The Chi-squre test found a significant association between the number of individuals detected per species and the citizen science approach. Given this result, I next examined the standardized Chi-square test residuals to determine which data set and species are the biggest contributors to rejecting the null hypothesis. 

## What do the test residuals say? 

We next examined the Chi-square test residuals. Residuals with large absolute values (typically greater than 2 or less than -2) indicate categories that contribute more to the chi-square statistic. Absolute values less than 2 indicate categories that do not contribute to the chi-square statistic.

```{r warning=FALSE, echo=FALSE}
# Calculate Pearson residuals
residuals <- chi_square_result$residuals

# Print residuals
print(residuals)

# Identify cells with large residuals
significant_cells <- which(abs(residuals) > 2, arr.ind = TRUE)

# Convert residuals to a dataframe for plotting
res_df <- as.data.frame(as.table(residuals))

# Create a heatmap of residuals
ggplot(res_df, aes(Var1, Var2, fill = Freq)) +
  geom_tile(color = "white") +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = "blue", high = "red", mid = "white", midpoint = 0, limit = c(-12, 12)) +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.2f", Freq)), color = "black", angle=90) +
  labs(x = "Species", y = "Data set", title = "Residuals of Chi-Square Test") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 90, hjust = 1))
```

Chi-square test residuals that are >2 in the Pollinator Pursuit project was associated with nine species/species groups: B. centralis, B. flavifrons, B. occidentalis, B. rufocinctus, and B. vancouverensis/bifarius; and in four species associated with the iNaturalist project: B. griseocollis, B. huntii, and B. morrisoni (Figure 1B). Based on X2 residuals, five species (i.e., B. appositus, B. fervidus, B. insularis, B. nevadensis, B. pensylvanicus) did not have an influence on the X2 test statistic. Of species that are listed as "Endangered" by the IUCN, B. occidentalis was detected more in the Utah Pollinator Pursuit project than in iNaturalist project, whereas B. morrisoni was detected more in the iNaturalist project than the Utah Pollinator Pursuit project. 

Interesting way to look at it, but wants to explore more spatial aspects of this. Both projects are constrained by bias, the bias is going to be different because of UPP smaller # of volunteers; whereas iNAT less constraint, wide open to anybody (is it possible to get users); less deliberate; articulate the number of folks who contribute iNAT data versus UPP. 

## Map the Utah Pollinator Pursuit and iNaturalist data sets.
The data sets are mapped to the grid system established by the Xerces Society for Invertebrate Conservation Utah Bumble Bee Atlas. The grid systems was provided by Amy Dolan, Endangered Species Conservation Biologist for the Xerces Society.

  geom_sf(data = upp_sf_points, aes(color = factor(`Bombus species`)), size = 3) +
  geom_sf_text(data = kml_data, aes(label = Name), 
               size = 4, color = "black", nudge_y = 0.01) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(title = "Utah Pollinator Pursuit observations in Utah (2020-2023)",
       color = "Species",
       x = "Longitude",
       y = "Latitude")

Fig2b<-ggsave("Figures/Fig2b.png", plot = UtahPP_plot, 
       width = 10, height = 8, units = "in")

# Rarefaction analysis for iNaturalist (Fig5)
```{r warning=FALSE, include=FALSE}

# Count the combinations of Category1 and Category2 for the Utah Pollinator Pursuit data merged with the KML file.
merged_sf_counts <- merged_sf %>%
  count(Name, `Bombus species`)

wide_counts <- merged_sf_counts %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = `Bombus species`, values_from = n, values_fill = list(n = 0))

wide_counts$geometry<-NULL

summarized_df <- wide_counts %>%
  group_by(Name) %>%
  summarise(across(where(is.numeric), sum, .names = "{.col}"))

summarized_df <- summarized_df[summarized_df$Name != "CLOSED", ]
nrow(summarized_df)
clean_df <- na.omit(summarized_df)
nrow(summarized_df)

summarized_df <-t(summarized_df)
colnames(summarized_df) <- as.character(unlist(summarized_df[1, ]))
summarized_df <- summarized_df[-1, ]

# Drop the last column
summarized_df <- summarized_df[ , -ncol(summarized_df)]
is.matrix(summarized_df)

# Check if matrix is numeric
all_numeric <- all(apply(summarized_df, 2, is.numeric))  # Check column-wise

if (!all_numeric) {
  mat <- matrix(as.numeric(summarized_df), ncol = ncol(summarized_df))
}

rownames(mat) <- rownames(summarized_df)
colnames(mat) <- colnames(summarized_df)

# Filter rows where the sum is not equal to 1
df_filtered <- mat[rowSums(mat) != 1, ] #WORKS so far.

# Calculate column sums
column_sums <- colSums(mat) 
column_sums

# Remove columns that sum to 1
mat_test <- mat[, column_sums != 1]
ncol(mat)
ncol(mat_test) #WORKS

# Calculate column sums
column_sums <- colSums(mat_test)
column_sums #WORKS

nrow(df_filtered)
df_filtered <- mat[rowSums(mat) != 0, ]
nrow(df_filtered) #WORKS

# Function to identify columns with only one non-zero element
remove_columns <- function(mat) {
  # Apply a function to each column to check for columns with exactly one non-zero element
  cols_to_keep <- apply(mat, 2, function(col) sum(col != 0) != 1)
  # Return the matrix without the columns with exactly one non-zero element
  return(mat[, cols_to_keep])
}

# Remove columns with only one non-zero element
result_matrix <- remove_columns(mat_test)
ncol(mat_test)
ncol(result_matrix) #WORKS
# Calculate column sums

column_sums <- colSums(result_matrix)
column_sums
# write.csv(result_matrix, "/Users/jonathankoch/Library/CloudStorage/Box-Box/0_Collaborative Projects/Amanda Barth/Barth_TeamUtahBombus/0_WorkingAnalysis/Data_v2/0 Final Figures/upp_gridspecies.csv")
```


```{r warning=FALSE, include=FALSE}
file.remove("Figures/Fig5.png")

# Estimate species richness for the Utah Pollinator Pursuit Data
iNEXT_out <- iNEXT(result_matrix, datatype = "abundance")
plot <- suppressWarnings(ggiNEXT(iNEXT_out))
ggsave("Figures/Fig5.png", plot = plot, 
       width = 10, height = 8, units = "in")
```

## How well sampled are each grid square based on rarefaction?

To answer this question, I used the iNEXT package in R. The iNEXT package estimates species richness and diversity (Simpson and Shannon Index) for a sample site.

## Rarefaction of the Utah Pollinator Pursuit data set.

The following graph represents species diversity rarefaction curves for each grid square assigned to Utah by the Xerces Society for Invertebrate Conservation to survey bumble bees in Utah. The data set being examined is the Utah Pollinator Pursuit data. Most grid squares did not achieve an asymptotic curve demonstrating that the grid square likley has not been sampled enough to detect all the likely species in the grid square. Thus, there is a lot of opportunity for continued sampling of bumble bees with the single data set.

Of the 40 grid squares sampled, the graph suggests that 3 grid squares likely were well sampled for all known species as the curves reach an asymptotic curve (i.e., 8.8% of the grid squares are well sampled) prior to extrapolation (dashed line). The well-sampled grid squares include UT_18, UT_13, UT_14. 

***Utah Pollinator Pursuit species diversity rarefaction curve***

```{r warning=FALSE, include=FALSE}
UtahPP_iNEXTEst <- as.data.frame(iNEXT_out$iNextEst$size_based)

UtahPP_filter <- UtahPP_iNEXTEst %>% filter(Method=="Rarefaction" & m>150)
unique(UtahPP_filter$Assemblage) 

# only 1 grid cell likely approached a complete inventory of bumble bee species. This cell in Salt lake City, Utah.
```

### Synthesis of rarefaction analyses

The Utah Pollinator Pursuit data set set appears to have achieved a species diversity (SD) asymptotic curve beyond (including extrapolated SD) at 150 observations in the following grid cells: UT_13 (Vernal), UT_18 (Salt Lake City), UT_24 (South Salt Lake City) and UT_62 (St. George). The iNaturalist data set appears to have reached an SD asymptotic curve (including extrapolated SD) at 150 observations with the following grid cells: UT_18 (Salt Lake City) and UT_24 (South Salt Lake City). Our data suggests there is a continued need to expand community science initiatives beyond populated areas. Targeted initiatives or adoption of a grid square by community scientist and stakeholders will increase approach to an asymptotic curve of species diversity.

# County Analysis
```{r}
# Replace "your_shapefile.shp" with the path to your shapefile
shapefile <- st_read("UtahCountyBoundaries_6245553605277884471")
st_crs(coordinates_sf)
st_crs(shapefile)
shapefile_transformed <- st_transform(shapefile, crs = st_crs(coordinates_sf))

# Make sure the two files have same CRS
st_crs(shapefile_transformed)
st_crs(coordinates_sf)

result <- st_join(coordinates_sf, shapefile_transformed, left = TRUE)
nrow(result)
df_all <-cbind(df_all,result)
df_all <-as.data.frame(df_all)
df_all <- subset(df_all, select = -geometry)

# Create a table of count data across species and data set type.
df_county_count <- df_all %>%
  group_by(NAME,source,POP_LASTCE) %>%
  summarise(count = n()) %>%
  arrange(desc(count))
df_county_count <- df_county_count %>% drop_na()

# seperate out by dataset
county_inat <- df_county_count %>%
  filter(source=="iNat")
plot(county_inat$POP_LASTCE, county_inat$count)
cor.test(county_inat$POP_LASTCE, county_inat$count, method="spearman")
nrow(county_inat)
# seperate out by dataset
county_UtahPP <- df_county_count %>%
  filter(source=="UtahPP")
plot(county_UtahPP$POP_LASTCE, county_UtahPP$count)
cor.test(county_UtahPP$POP_LASTCE, county_UtahPP$count, method="spearman")
```
